text: Design a microservices architecture in Rust.
expected_response: Decompose into independently deployable services, each owning its data store and communicating through async message passing. Use an API Gateway as the entry point, routing requests to services. Apply Event Sourcing so services publish domain events to a broker for loose coupling. Structure each service with hexagonal architecture: domain logic at center, adapters on the boundary.

text: Design a microservices architecture in Python.
expected_response: Structure the system as a collection of small, focused services communicating via REST or message queues. Use a Proxy Gateway to handle authentication, rate limiting, and routing. Each service follows the Repository pattern internally, separating domain logic from data access. Apply the Observer pattern for cross-service event notification through a message broker like RabbitMQ or Redis Streams, so services react to events they care about without direct coupling.

text: How do Observer and Event-Driven Architecture work together?
expected_response: Observer defines local one-to-many notification within a single process. Event-Driven Architecture scales this across service boundaries via a message broker. Together, local state changes propagate globally without tight coupling: Observer handles in-process notification, the event bus handles cross-process distribution.

text: Combine Proxy and Circuit Breaker for resilient service communication.
expected_response: Wrap each remote call in a Proxy that integrates a Circuit Breaker tracking failure rates. When failures exceed a threshold, the circuit opens and the Proxy returns a cached response instead. After a cooldown, it transitions to half-open for a trial request. This isolates failures and provides graceful degradation without changing the client interface.

text: Use Strategy pattern with Factory for configurable algorithms at runtime.
expected_response: Define each algorithm variant as a Strategy implementation behind a common interface. Use a Factory to instantiate the correct strategy based on runtime configuration, user preference, or environment variables. The client receives the strategy through dependency injection and calls it without knowing which variant was selected. This separates algorithm selection (Factory) from algorithm execution (Strategy), making both independently extensible.

text: Design a plugin system using Component, Flyweight, and Factory patterns.
expected_response: Define a Plugin trait that all extensions implement with lifecycle hooks: init, execute, shutdown. Use a Factory to instantiate plugins from configuration, isolating the host from concrete types. Apply Flyweight for shared immutable state across instances, reducing memory. The host iterates over registered components through the uniform interface.

text: Apply CQRS with Event Sourcing for an audit-compliant system.
expected_response: Separate write model from read model. Commands mutate state by appending events to an immutable store rather than updating records. The read side subscribes and projects events into optimized views. This provides a complete audit trail, enables temporal queries via event replay, and allows independent scaling of reads and writes.

text: How do Decorator and Chain of Responsibility compose for middleware pipelines?
expected_response: Each middleware layer is a Decorator that wraps the next handler, adding behavior before and after delegation. The Chain of Responsibility links these decorators in sequence: authentication checks first, then rate limiting, then logging, then the actual handler. Each layer can short-circuit the chain by returning early or pass the request down. This composes cross-cutting concerns cleanly, with each middleware independently testable and reorderable.

text: Design a notification system combining Observer, Template Method, and Adapter.
expected_response: Observer tracks subscribers and notifies them on events. Each channel implements a Template Method defining the send workflow: validate, format, dispatch, log. Channels wrapping third-party APIs use Adapter to translate the internal interface. Adding a channel means one Adapter and one Template Method subclass, with zero changes to the Observer core.

text: Combine Hexagonal Architecture with Repository and Dependency Injection.
expected_response: Place domain logic at the center with no external dependencies. Define ports as trait interfaces for use cases and data access. Repository implements the outbound port, abstracting database operations. Dependency Injection wires concrete adapters into ports at startup. The domain stays testable in isolation via mock adapters.

text: Design a real-time dashboard using MVC and Observer.
expected_response: The Model holds application state and metrics data. Views subscribe to the Model as Observers, automatically re-rendering when state changes. The Controller handles user interactions (filter changes, time range selection) and updates the Model accordingly. When new data arrives via WebSocket, the Model updates its state and notifies all subscribed Views, which re-render their charts and tables without the Controller needing to orchestrate each view update.

text: Build a component library using Compound Components and Render Props.
expected_response: Compound Components share implicit state through context. A parent manages state while children render specific parts: Menu manages open/close, Menu.Trigger renders the button, Menu.Items the dropdown. Render Props expose state via a function prop for custom rendering. Together they create opinionated yet fully customizable components.

text: Implement a form system using State Machine and Validation Chain patterns.
expected_response: Model the form lifecycle as a state machine: idle, editing, validating, submitting, success, error. Validation uses a Chain of Responsibility where each validator checks one rule and either passes or short-circuits. The state machine ensures validation before submission and prevents double-submits.

text: Design a theming system using Strategy and Context patterns.
expected_response: Each theme is a Strategy providing color tokens, typography, spacing, and variant styles. A Theme Context holds the active strategy and propagates it to all components. Switching themes swaps the strategy, triggering re-renders with new tokens. Nested contexts allow overrides for specific subtrees.
